summary: This document defines an RDAP extension called "geofeed1" to show that an RDAP server hosts geofeed URLs for its IP network objects. It also defines a new media type and link relation for the link objects in responses.

plainLanguage.summary: A geofeed is a list saying roughly where addresses are used. This lets the lookup service point to that list in a standard way.

questions: how to find ip geofeed in rdap
what is an rdap geofeed link
subtitle: How an RDAP server points to the geofeed file for an IP network, using a new link type and extension.

tldr.problem: Geofeed URLs could be published through RPSL, but the Regional Internet Registries now run RDAP as the successor service, so RDAP needed an equivalent way to expose them.
tldr.mechanism: An RDAP IP network object may carry a link object with rel set to geofeed and type application/geofeed+csv. A server signals support by listing the geofeed1 extension identifier in rdapConformance.
tldr.outcome: Clients can find a network's geofeed URL through RDAP and, when the extension is present, infer that a missing link means no geofeed data exists for that object.

today: RFC 9877 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Geofeeds Meet RDAP
sections.content:
RFC 8805 and RFC 9632 describe the IP geolocation feed, commonly called a geofeed, and how to find and access it. RFC 9632 explains how a registry can publish geofeed URLs through an RPSL service. The Regional Internet Registries have deployed RDAP services as successors to RPSL for Internet number resources, and keeping feature parity supports clients moving from RPSL to RDAP.

This RFC therefore specifies how geofeed URLs are reached through RDAP. It defines the geofeed1 extension, a new media type and a new link relation type. Fetching and using the geofeed data is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: There is already a list that tells roughly where internet addresses are used. Now the address lookup service has an official way to point to that list.

sections.title: The Geofeed Link Object
sections.content:
An RDAP server that hosts geofeed URLs may add link objects to the links member of an IP network object. Every RDAP link object needs value, rel and href. For a geofeed link, type is also RECOMMENDED. The geofeed-specific parts are:

  • rel: the new link relation geofeed.
  • href: the HTTPS URL of the geofeed file.
  • type: application/geofeed+csv.

An IP network object MAY contain zero or more geofeed links, though typically it has zero or one. More than one is for when the server can offer the data in multiple languages, and then it SHOULD provide hreflang members. Otherwise it SHOULD NOT return more than one.
sections.plainLanguage: The lookup answer gets a little signpost labeled geofeed with the web address of the list. Usually there is one signpost, or none.

sections.title: The Media Type Choice
sections.content:
RFC 9632 requires a geofeed file to be UTF-8 comma-separated values with optional trailing comment lines that carry the RPKI signature. The text/csv type looks like a fit at first glance.

The RFC prefers a new application type because the common use is to process the data in an application before doing IP address lookups, not to show it to a person. So it registers application/geofeed+csv and a new +csv structured syntax suffix.
sections.plainLanguage: The list looks like a plain spreadsheet file, but programs mostly use it rather than people reading it. So it gets its own special file label.

sections.title: The geofeed1 Extension
sections.content:
A server that hosts geofeed URLs for its IP network objects and returns them in link objects uses the extension identifier geofeed1. It MUST list it in the rdapConformance array for any lookup or search response containing an IP network object, and in the help response. The "1" marks version 1; new versions will use different identifiers.

If the identifier is listed, then for any IP network object where the server has a geofeed URL and is able to return it (not compelled to omit it by regulation or similar), the server MUST include the geofeed link object.

A server may use the media type and link relation without the extension identifier. The extra value of the identifier is the signal to clients: if an IP network object arrives without a geofeed link, the client can infer that no geofeed data is available for it.
sections.plainLanguage: A server can put up a sign saying it always shows the geofeed signpost when it has one. If you then see no signpost, you know there is no list.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
A lookup returns the most-specific IP network object covering the requested range. That object may lack a geofeed link while a less-specific parent has one. Clients should consider fetching parent objects, recursively, when the first response has none. Server operators should consider interfaces that let resource holders provide links for all their networks.

Resource holders often keep one geofeed file for all their resources and point every network object at it. A client that follows a geofeed link MUST ignore any entry whose address range is outside the IP network object's range. Clients MUST NOT do frequent real-time lookups, to avoid undue load on RDAP and geofeed servers. Using the RDAP bootstrap process (RFC 9224) directs clients to the server that is authoritative for the resources.
sections.plainLanguage: If the small address block has no signpost, check the bigger block it belongs to. Ignore list lines about addresses that are not yours, and do not ask over and over.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
The privacy considerations of RFC 9632 apply. In particular, the publisher of a geofeed file MUST take care not to expose the location of any individual. Registry operators should check whether the laws where they operate, which often restrict personal data, permit this functionality.

A geofeed file MUST be referenced with an HTTPS URL and may contain an RPKI signature. Apart from the considerations in RFC 9632 and the RDAP specifications, the RFC adds no new security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The list must never reveal where a particular person lives, and the web address must use the secure kind of link.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has made four registrations:

  • RDAP Extensions registry: geofeed1.
  • Link Relations registry: geofeed.
  • Media Types registry: application/geofeed+csv. No charset parameter is used because geofeed content is always UTF-8.
  • Structured Syntax Suffixes registry: +csv.
sections.plainLanguage: The official name lists now include the new extension name, link label, file type and suffix.
